Summary

This paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in linear MDPs, where an agent has access to both an offline dataset and online interaction. The main goal is to show that hybrid RL can provably outperform the best-known guarantees for purely offline or purely online learning without relying on single-policy concentrability. The paper proposes two algorithms:

1. RAPPEL: an online-to-offline method that uses reward-agnostic exploration (via OPTCOV) to augment the offline dataset, then runs a pessimistic offline RL algorithm.
2. HYRULE: an offline-to-online method that warm-starts a nearly minimax-optimal online RL algorithm using offline data.

The claimed contributions are improved PAC/error and regret guarantees in linear MDPs, with bounds that are never worse than the corresponding offline-only or online-only guarantees and can be strictly better depending on the partition of the feature space into “offline-covered” and “online-needed” components.

Overall assessment

The paper addresses an important and timely question in hybrid RL theory. The central question—whether hybrid RL can break the apparent sample barriers of offline-only and online-only RL in non-tabular settings without single-policy concentrability—is significant. The paper is ambitious and technically substantial. The proposed decomposition into offline and online partitions is interesting, and the attempt to obtain improvements for both PAC and regret settings in linear MDPs is valuable.

That said, I have substantial concerns about the clarity, precision, and in some places the credibility of the theoretical claims as currently presented. The paper appears to contain several conceptual and technical ambiguities, some assumptions that seem stronger or less innocuous than advertised, and some comparisons that are not always fully apples-to-apples. The experimental section is also fairly limited and does not convincingly validate the theory. My overall view is that the paper has promising ideas and may contain meaningful technical progress, but it needs significant revision before I would be comfortable endorsing the claims at face value.

Strengths

1. Important problem
The paper tackles a genuinely interesting open direction in RL theory: hybrid RL beyond tabular settings and without single-policy concentrability. This is a worthwhile target for a theory conference.

2. Two complementary settings
It is a strength that the paper addresses both PAC-style policy learning and regret minimization, rather than only one of them. The distinction between online-to-offline and offline-to-online approaches is well motivated.

3. Potentially meaningful technical ideas
The partition-based analysis into offline and online subspaces, and the use of projected dimensions/concentrability quantities, seem potentially useful. The claimed sharpening from ambient dimension d to d_on and c_off(X_off) is conceptually appealing.

4. Computational efficiency
The algorithms are based on known polynomial-time primitives, which is preferable to purely information-theoretic results.

5. Honest discussion of some limitations
The paper does acknowledge burn-in costs, the difficulty of achieving H^3 in offline linear MDPs, and the lack of a single algorithm that simultaneously dominates both offline-only and online-only rates.

Main concerns

1. The assumptions and “no concentrability” message are somewhat misleading

A central message is that the results avoid single-policy concentrability. Formally this is true, but the replacement assumptions deserve much more scrutiny.

For RAPPEL, Assumption 2 requires that for any partition, c_on(X_on) < infinity, equivalently that there exists a policy whose projected covariance on the online partition is full rank at every stage. This is presented as mild and “essentially achievable” via feature transformation. I find this discussion problematic.

First, requiring this for any partition is quite strong. Second, the claim that this is achievable “for any linear MDP via a transformation of the features” is not obvious and may be misleading: projecting onto nonzero singular directions of an offline covariance matrix does not by itself imply the existence of an exploration policy that achieves the required stage-wise full-rank projected covariance over the online partition. This seems to conflate representational rank with controllable reachability/explorability. In RL, the issue is not only whether features span a subspace, but whether trajectories induced by some policy can excite those directions at each stage.

More broadly, the paper replaces standard concentrability with partition-dependent quantities c_off and c_on. These are still coverage assumptions, just in a more refined form. That is fine, but the exposition should be more careful not to oversell the absence of assumptions on data quality. In particular, Theorem 1 depends on choosing a good partition and on an exploration assumption that may be nontrivial in practice.

2. The partition is existential in theory but operationally unclear in practice

Many of the main bounds are stated for every partition and then interpreted via the existence of a favorable partition. However, the algorithms do not always know the partition.

For HYRULE, the adaptivity claim is attractive: the algorithm is partition-agnostic and the regret bound takes an infimum over partitions. That is nice if correct.

For RAPPEL, however, the algorithm requires choosing the OPTCOV tolerance, and the discussion says this effectively requires choosing d_on or estimating it from the offline spectrum. This weakens the practical significance of the partition-based guarantee. The theory seems to rely on a partition-dependent tolerance, but the algorithm does not specify how to choose it in a principled way without access to the unknown best partition. The paper acknowledges this, but the issue is more serious than presented: the strongest theorem is not fully algorithmically instantiated unless one knows enough about the partition structure.

3. Theoretical statements are difficult to parse and sometimes appear inconsistent

There are several places where the theorem statements and surrounding discussion are hard to reconcile.

For example, Theorem 1 gives a minimum of two bounds:
- one with H^4 and linear dependence on c_off and d_on,
- one with H^3 but quadratic dependence on c_off and d_on through min terms / alpha terms.

Then later the paper summarizes this as a sample complexity of
c_off d H^3 min{c_off, H}/eps^2 + d_on d H^3 min{d_on, H}/eps^2.
This summary is plausible but not immediate from the theorem as written, and the role of alpha_off, alpha_on, and N = N_off + N_on is not very transparent. The theorem statement itself is cumbersome and hard to interpret.

Similarly, Theorem 2 assumes N_on, N_off = \tilde{\Omega}(d^{13} H^{14}), which is enormous. This is a major caveat, yet the abstract and introduction emphasize “breaking sample size barriers” and “sharpest guarantees.” While asymptotic improvements in the leading term may still be meaningful, such huge burn-in/sample lower bounds substantially weaken the practical and even conceptual impact. The paper should foreground this much more clearly.

4. Comparison to lower bounds and “breaks barriers” framing is too strong

The title and abstract strongly suggest that the paper overcomes minimax lower bounds in a robust sense. But the actual results are partition-dependent upper bounds that can improve over offline-only or online-only rates under favorable structure. This is interesting, but “breaks sample size barriers” sounds stronger than what is rigorously established.

In particular:
- For RAPPEL, the improvement over offline-only is immediate because adding online data improves covariance. But this is not the same as proving a new minimax characterization of hybrid RL.
- For HYRULE, the regret bound improves over online-only when N_off is large and c_off is favorable. Again, this is a conditional improvement, not a universal domination result.
- The paper does not provide matching lower bounds for the hybrid setting in linear MDPs, so claims like “tightest theoretical guarantees currently available” should be softened unless carefully qualified as “best known upper bounds.”

5. Novelty relative to prior work is somewhat incremental algorithmically

Algorithmically, both methods are combinations/modifications of existing ingredients:
- RAPPEL = OPTCOV + LinPEVI-ADV+
- HYRULE = warm-started LSVI-UCB++

The novelty is primarily in the analysis. That is acceptable for a theory paper, but then the analysis must be especially clean and convincing. At present, the presentation makes it hard to verify exactly what is new and where the main technical gains come from. The paper repeatedly cites “novel truncation arguments” and sharper projected-dimension lemmas, but the main text does not isolate these contributions crisply enough.

6. Experimental validation is weak

The experiments are not strong enough for the scope of the claims.

- Only one environment is used: a scaled-down Tetris benchmark.
- The implementations do not actually use the exact algorithms from the theory. The paper substitutes LSVI-UCB for FORCE inside OPTCOV and LinPEVI-ADV for LinPEVI-ADV+, and uses LSVI-UCB++ “as-is” for Algorithm 2. This is understandable from an engineering perspective, but it weakens the empirical support considerably.
- The experiments do not test the key theoretical quantities or regimes, such as varying N_off/N_on, varying coverage quality systematically, or demonstrating scaling with d_on/c_off.
- There is no comparison against the most relevant theoretical baselines from prior hybrid RL work in linear settings, beyond online-only/offline-only variants.
- The number of trials is small in Figure 3.

As a result, the experiments are more anecdotal than confirmatory.

7. Presentation quality needs improvement

The paper is often difficult to read. Some issues:
- The notation is heavy and sometimes inconsistent.
- Several claims are buried in long paragraphs without enough intuition.
- There are typographical issues and awkward phrasing throughout.
- Some theorem assumptions and consequences are not cleanly separated.
- The references to equations and lemmas are dense enough that the main narrative becomes hard to follow.

A few examples:
- The definition of N*(tau) is hard to parse and not well motivated in the main text.
- The proof sketches are too compressed to be genuinely illuminating.
- The discussion around Assumption 2 and feature transformations is especially confusing.
- There are occasional grammatical issues and duplicated punctuation.

Detailed comments and questions

1. On Lemma 1
The claim that for any partition, c_on(X_on) <= d_on is surprisingly strong. Since c_on is defined via an inf over policies of inverse minimum eigenvalues, this seems to require a nontrivial geometric/exploration argument. I would like the authors to explain much more clearly in the main text why this is true in linear MDPs and under what exact assumptions. As stated, it feels stronger than standard coverability facts.

2. On the existence of a partition with c_off(X_off)=O(d)
This existential statement is important for the claimed worst-case guarantees. But what is this partition concretely? Is it data-dependent, MDP-dependent, or purely existential? If it is purely existential, how should one interpret the practical relevance of the bound?

3. On Theorem 1 and the role of OPTCOV
The theorem depends on choosing tau appropriately. But tau depends on quantities involving d_on and c_off(X_off), which are not known. Is there a parameter-free or adaptive version? If not, the algorithmic significance of the theorem is limited.

4. On the burn-in/sample assumptions
Theorem 2 requires N_on, N_off = \tilde{\Omega}(d^{13}H^{14}). This is extremely large. Is this purely an artifact of proof techniques inherited from He et al. plus the truncation argument, or is some part essential? Can the authors isolate the dominant source of this requirement?

5. On the offline term in Theorem 2
The regret bound contains sqrt(c_off(X_off)^2 d H^3 N_on^2 / N_off). The square on c_off is somewhat unattractive and appears worse than one might hope from analogy with the online term. Is this unavoidable? The paper hints that this comes from the truncation/eigenvalue control argument. It would help to discuss whether this is believed to be an artifact.

6. On comparisons to prior work
Some comparisons seem selective. For example, the paper compares RAPPEL mainly to Wagenmaker and Pacchiano (2023), but since RAPPEL uses a strong offline RL subroutine, it would be useful to compare more explicitly to simply running offline RL on the offline data plus naive online exploration, or to other hybrid baselines that do not use reward-agnostic exploration.

7. On the “reward-agnostic hybrid RL” claim
The paper suggests RAPPEL also solves reward-agnostic hybrid RL because exploration is reward-agnostic and the final offline learner can be rerun for different rewards. This is plausible, but only if the reward remains linear in the same features and the collected data includes the necessary reward observations or can be relabeled. This should be stated more carefully.

8. On the typo correction in Algorithm 2
The footnote about a likely typo in He et al. is useful, but if the present analysis depends on this correction, the paper should be more explicit about whether the theorem is proved for the corrected algorithm or for the original published one.

9. On the tabular corollary
Corollary 1 is interesting, but I would like a clearer comparison to Li et al. (2023b). Does the corollary recover the same qualitative improvement in the tabular setting, or is it weaker/stronger in some regimes?

10. On computational efficiency
The paper repeatedly says the algorithms are computationally efficient when the action space is finite. That is fair, but for RAPPEL the practical cost of OPTCOV may still be substantial. Some discussion of actual runtime or implementation burden would help, especially since the experiments use substitutes.

Suggestions for improvement

1. Tone down the title and strongest claims
I would strongly recommend softening “breaks sample size barriers” unless the authors can more carefully justify this phrasing. Something like “Provable gains from hybrid reinforcement learning in linear MDPs” would be more precise.

2. Clarify assumptions and avoid overselling
The paper should explicitly distinguish:
- no single-policy concentrability,
- but still requiring partition-dependent coverage/explorability assumptions.
The discussion of Assumption 2 should be rewritten carefully.

3. Improve theorem presentation
The main theorems should be restated in a cleaner, more interpretable form, perhaps with a simplified corollary highlighting the main regimes. Right now the statements are too cumbersome.

4. Better explain the partition framework
The paper should include a more intuitive explanation of what kinds of offline datasets induce small c_off and small d_on, and perhaps a toy example illustrating the partition.

5. Strengthen experiments
At minimum:
- vary N_off and N_on systematically,
- compare against stronger baselines,
- show sensitivity to offline data quality,
- if possible, include a synthetic linear MDP where d_on and c_off can be controlled.

6. Be more explicit about what is algorithmic versus existential
For RAPPEL especially, the dependence on unknown partition/tolerance should be highlighted as a limitation.

7. Tighten writing and notation
The paper would benefit from substantial editing for readability.

Recommendation

Weak reject.

Rationale

I think the paper is addressing an important problem and likely contains nontrivial technical ideas. The partition-based perspective and the attempt to obtain improvements in both PAC and regret settings are promising. However, in its current form, the paper overstates some claims, relies on assumptions that are not as benign as suggested, presents the theory in a way that is difficult to verify, and provides limited empirical support. If the proofs are correct, this may well be a valuable contribution after revision, but I do not think the current presentation is strong enough for acceptance.

Confidence

Medium. I am reasonably confident in my concerns about framing, assumptions, and presentation. My confidence in the ultimate correctness of the technical proofs is lower because the paper is dense and many key arguments are deferred to the appendix.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in episodic linear MDPs, where an agent has both offline data and online interaction. It proposes two computationally efficient algorithms: RAPPEL, an online-to-offline method that performs reward-agnostic exploration to augment offline data before running pessimistic offline RL for PAC guarantees; and HYRULE, an offline-to-online method that warm-starts a nearly minimax-optimal online RL algorithm with offline estimates for regret minimization. The main claims are that these methods avoid single-policy concentrability assumptions, improve over prior hybrid RL bounds in linear MDPs, and can outperform the best known offline-only or online-only guarantees depending on the objective. Theoretical results provide partition-dependent bounds in terms of partial offline coverage and online exploration dimensions, and experiments on a scaled-down Tetris environment qualitatively support benefits over purely offline or purely online baselines.
strengths: Addresses an important open question in hybrid RL beyond the tabular setting, specifically for linear MDPs without single-policy concentrability.
Provides two complementary algorithmic paradigms, one for PAC learning and one for regret minimization, which broadens the paper's scope and relevance.
Theoretical guarantees are stronger than prior hybrid RL results for linear MDPs, especially in horizon dependence and partition-adaptive dimension dependence.
The partition-based analysis using offline-covered and online-explored subspaces is conceptually appealing and helps explain when hybrid RL can improve over pure offline or online learning.
Algorithms are computationally efficient in discrete action spaces by leveraging existing efficient subroutines.
The paper is well situated in prior literature and clearly articulates what is new relative to existing offline, online, and hybrid RL work.
Numerical experiments, though limited, are aligned with the theoretical motivation and illustrate potential gains from hybridization even with poor offline data.
weaknesses: The assumptions and guarantees are quite complex, and some of the practical relevance of the partition quantities c_off(X_off) and d_on is unclear because they may be difficult to estimate or optimize in real problems.
For RAPPEL, the user must choose a tolerance or effectively a partition-related quantity, which weakens adaptivity and practical usability.

The burn-in/sample requirements are very large and sometimes extreme, especially the HYRULE condition N_on, N_off = \tilde{\Omega}(d^{13}H^{14}), which limits practical significance of the regret theorem.
The experimental section is relatively modest and uses simplified implementations rather than the exact proposed algorithms/subroutines, making empirical validation weaker than the theory.

Some claimed improvements are qualified and not fully clean; for example, the PAC bound still falls short of the conjectured sharper form, and improvements depend on favorable partitions or sample regimes.

The presentation occasionally overstates practical achievability of assumptions, such as feature transformations ensuring explorable projected covariates, without fully discussing whether this preserves the intended problem structure.
There is limited discussion of how one would select or approximate the best partition in practice, despite the theory hinging on partition-dependent quantities.
soundness_issues: Theoretical contributions appear technically substantial and largely plausible, but several key claims rely on nontrivial lemmas deferred to appendices, making full verification difficult from the main text alone.

Assumption 2 for RAPPEL is strong and somewhat awkwardly phrased ('for any partition'), and the claim that it is achievable in practice via feature transformation may require more justification; it is not obvious this is innocuous in general.
The regret theorem for HYRULE requires extremely large lower bounds on sample sizes, suggesting the proof may be loose; while not invalid, this weakens the practical meaning of the result.

The experiments do not exactly implement the proposed algorithms (substituting LSVI-UCB for FORCE inside OPTCOV and LinPEVI-ADV for LinPEVI-ADV+), so empirical evidence is only indirect support for the stated methods.

The paper notes a suspected typo in a cited prior work and modifies the variance floor accordingly; this seems reasonable, but such a change should be justified carefully since it affects the instantiated algorithm and proof dependencies.
